title: Stored Energy
story: Second shift, Line 4, a rush order. The case packer jams. Its air dump valve has been tagged out of service for three weeks. Rusty hits the E-stop and reaches in. The pusher still has air behind it.
chain: An E-stop stops the motion. It does not lock out the energy.
Air left in the lines was never bled off or blocked.
A broken dump valve was worked around for three weeks.
The rush order set the pace, not the procedure.
checks: Every energy source isolated: electric, air, hydraulic, gravity
Your own lock and tag on each point
Stored energy released or blocked
Try to start it: verify zero energy
Broken isolation device? Stop and report it
stop_when: A hand past a guard on an E-stop alone. "It'll only take a second." A tag that's been hanging for weeks. One lock for the whole crew.
emergency: Keep the machine stopped and the energy isolated. Call for help and first aid. Don't reach in after them.
questions: Where on our floor do we rely on an E-stop instead of a lock?
Which of our machines still hold energy after shutdown: air, springs, gravity?
Which tags have been hanging longer than a week, and who owns fixing them?
references: 29 CFR 1910.147, The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout) — ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.147
OSHA Lockout/Tagout topic page and Top 10 most-cited standards — osha.gov/control-hazardous-energy · osha.gov/top10citedstandards

title: Six Feet Down
story: A sewer tie-in on a residential street. The trench box rental is late and the competent person is pulled to another job. The trench is over seven feet deep. Tito climbs in for "one joint." The wall comes down, and Ray goes in after him.
chain: The competent person was pulled to another site.
No box, shoring or sloping at seven feet.
Spoil piled at the edge; the ladder 40 feet away.
Rain, seep and a crack, and nobody re-inspected.
checks: 5 ft or deeper: box, shoring or sloping in place
Competent person on site and inspected today
Spoil and materials 2 ft back from the edge
A way out within 25 ft of the work
Re-inspected after rain, water or cracks
stop_when: Water weeping from a wall. Cracks along the top edge. Soil dropping in. A missing box. A competent person who's left the site.
emergency: Call 911. Keep everyone out and back from the edge. Shut down equipment. Wait for trained rescuers.
questions: If our competent person gets pulled away, who has the authority to close the trench?
On our jobs, how far from the edge do spoil and equipment actually sit?
What would we do in the first 60 seconds after a collapse?
references: OSHA Trenching and Excavation topic page (fatality data and resources) — osha.gov/trenching-excavation

title: The Tank
story: An air-locked pump in a lift-station wet well. The gas meter stays in the truck, and nobody writes a permit. Dale goes down. When he goes quiet, Andre goes after him. Hannah stays out and calls 911.
chain: No permit, so no plan, no attendant, no rescue.
No air test before entry, and no monitor during it.
The fading smell was taken as good news.
No retrieval line, so a partner went in instead.
checks: Permit written for this entry
Air tested from outside: O2, flammable, toxic
Meter calibrated, bump-tested, monitoring
Fresh air blowing in the whole time
Tripod, harness and line on the entrant
stop_when: A meter left in the truck. "It's just a five-minute job." A smell that fades. Anyone heading down after someone who's gone quiet.
emergency: Stay out. Call 911 and say it's a confined space. Use the retrieval line if one is rigged.
questions: Which spaces on our sites are permit spaces, and does everyone know it?
Where is our gas meter right now, and when was it last bump-tested?
If someone went down today, how would we get them out without sending anyone in?
references: NIOSH Publication 94-103, Worker Deaths in Confined Spaces — cdc.gov/niosh/docs/94-103

title: Eight Feet
story: A Phoenix reroof racing a hailstorm. Fall protection was cut from the bid, so the harnesses stay in the truck. The new apprentice asks about anchors and gets a laugh. Cody backs off an eight-foot porch roof onto concrete.
chain: Fall protection was cut from the bid to win the job.
Harnesses rode in the truck with no anchors on the roof.
The hailstorm set the pace, not the plan.
The apprentice asked, and the crew laughed.
checks_label: Before anyone works at the edge
checks: 6 ft+ (4 ft gen. industry; any height over dangerous equipment): guardrail, net or fall arrest
Rated anchors installed on the roof
Fall protection in the bid and budget
Storm coming? Stop early, don't rush
Material away from edges; never back up
stop_when: Harnesses in the truck. "It's only one story." Someone backing toward an edge. A new worker's question laughed off.
emergency: Call 911. Don't move them unless they're in more danger. Secure the area and the edge.
questions: Where do we work six feet up with nothing to stop a fall?
Who decides what fall protection goes in the bid?
When a new hire asks a safety question here, what actually happens?
references: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(13), Fall protection in residential construction (6 ft) — ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1926.501
1910.28(b)(1)(i) general industry, 4 ft; 1910.28(b)(6) and 1926.501(b)(8), dangerous equipment at any height — ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.28
